video_title: The Real AI Playbook: How to Use AI Better w/ @austin.marchese
gist: Austin Marchese, a former JP Morgan engineer who says his team's internal AI risk tool replaced Palantir's, explains why high cost-of-error and 'neck on the line' accountability force banks toward AI augmentation rather than automation, and lays out a spec-verifier-environment framework plus claude.md/skills practices for reliable LLM output. He argues AI now owns the execution layer that junior analysts performed, so finance workers must become outcome-owning 'financial engineers'; note he discloses a collaboration with Anthropic while recommending Claude 99% of the time. The transcript appears machine-translated, and the second half is audio-only.

themes.theme: AI adoption inside banks: cost of error and accountability

insights.claim: The guest led a JP Morgan team that built an internal AI-driven risk-identification tool which he says replaced a tool from Palantir.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Large banks are willing to build in-house AI tooling that displaces incumbent enterprise vendors like Palantir.
insights.quote: the team I led that replaced the tool they were building

insights.claim: In banks, law firms and accounting firms the high 'cost of a mistake' limits how far AI can be pushed, so successful deployments augment analyst workflows rather than automate them end to end.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Expect AI adoption in regulated financial and professional services to be incremental and augmentation-led, slowing the pace of headcount displacement there.

insights.claim: Resistance to AI among senior (40-50 year old) finance professionals stems from treating AI as a 'magic wand' and from unclear ownership when outputs are bad; reframing AI as a tool owned by an accountable human makes executives more receptive.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI rollouts hinge on governance and accountability design, not model capability alone.

insights.claim: Bank culture requires a 'neck on the line' (a named accountable person) for any process, and removing the human owner in favor of a pure AI tool is where enterprise implementation slows down.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop requirements cap near-term full automation in financial institutions and favor copilot-style products.

insights.claim: The guest argues AI adoption problems are the same at a Fortune 500 company and a 5-20 person startup, and should be solved one problem at a time from a scalability rather than automation perspective.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: AI value capture is a workflow-by-workflow process, implying gradual rather than step-change enterprise productivity gains.

insights.claim: Models exhibit a tendency to rush to a finished product, so an underspecified request like 'do my month-end accounting' may silently pick the wrong basis (e.g., cash vs. accrual).
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Unsupervised AI in finance workflows carries real error risk from unstated assumptions, reinforcing the need for human-defined specifications.

insights.claim: Effective AI use moves the human from the execution level to the 'architectural' level: write a specification defining what, how and why before handing execution to the AI.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Value in knowledge work shifts toward people who design and specify processes rather than execute them.

insights.claim: The guest's three-layer framework is specification, verifier and environment, and he claims doing all three puts a user ahead of about 80-90% of people.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: A simple, model-agnostic playbook for getting reliable output from LLMs in professional workflows.
insights.quote: if you just do these three levels, you will be ahead of about 80-90% of people

insights.claim: Asking the AI to 'interview me' during planning surfaces gaps in the user's own requirements, acting like an expert consultant in the room.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Cheap technique to reduce rework and error in AI-assisted analysis.

insights.claim: For verification, giving the model prior finished examples (e.g., 12 past monthly reports and a template) lets it check its own output before delivering it; the guest notes the newest models now self-verify by default.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Self-verification being built into frontier models increases their reliability for repetitive enterprise reporting tasks.

insights.claim: The environment layer means connecting the AI to data sources via built-in integrations such as Gmail, Outlook and Slack so it can actually pull the inputs it needs.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Connector/integration ecosystems are a key determinant of which AI assistant becomes embedded in workflows.

insights.claim: Loops are iterations between execution and the verifier, letting the AI self-correct before results reach the user; poor outputs usually reflect an underbuilt verification layer.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Agentic reliability is driven by verification design, a key lever for enterprise deployment.

insights.claim: Stuffing everything into claude.md raises token consumption on every exchange, hitting usage limits faster, and more context often produces worse results; instead point claude.md at context files ('gradual disclosure').
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Token economics and context discipline shape AI usage costs and output quality for power users and enterprises.
insights.quote: more context doesn't necessarily mean a better outcome. In fact, it can often mean a worse outcome

insights.claim: The guest calls Claude's skills his favorite feature by far, describing them as codified standard operating procedures that can be composed, e.g., a 'get monthly report data' skill pulling from QuickBooks, Excel and Slack, orchestrated by a higher-level 'generate monthly report' skill.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Skills/agent workflows that wire into business software point to deep workflow lock-in for AI platforms.

insights.claim: Skills are a primitive that exists across toolkits (ChatGPT has its own version), so the skill of building them is model-independent.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Workflow primitives are converging across AI vendors, limiting feature-based differentiation.

insights.claim: A rule of thumb credited to Matt Peak: if you keep 'sending back' AI output like a wrong restaurant order, that task should become a skill; you can then ask the AI to turn the conversation into a skill.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Practical filter for which workflows are worth automating, avoiding building unused tools.

themes.theme: Model choice: single-tool focus vs. switching

insights.claim: Contrary to common advice, the guest uses Claude and its newest model 99% of the time and advises professionals to pick one desktop tool and ignore new releases from rivals to avoid decision fatigue and an 'AI tool graveyard'.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Suggests user stickiness to a primary AI assistant may be high once workflows are built, favoring incumbents with strong ecosystems.
insights.quote: I use Claude and their newest model 99% of the time

insights.claim: The host uses Claude and ChatGPT most, Gemini somewhat, and Grok for scientific, statistical and analytical work and X data; both agree Grok's edge is real-time data from X.
insights.speaker: Ash Bennington (host)
insights.so_what: Grok's differentiation is perceived as data access (X) rather than general capability.

insights.claim: The guest discloses he is currently collaborating with Anthropic, and his channel has grown fast since April by targeting 30-60 year old professionals rather than get-rich-quick AI content.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: His strong Claude preference should be weighed against his commercial relationship with Anthropic; signals large demand among mid-career professionals for AI upskilling.

themes.theme: Junior roles and the future of finance careers

insights.claim: AI now owns the 'execution level' that junior roles used to perform, producing a flattening of roles across Wall Street and beyond.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Points to reduced junior hiring needs at banks and professional firms and margin leverage for incumbents.

insights.claim: Financial analysts should shift from analyst to 'financial engineer' mindset, because pulling numbers is being outsourced to AI and value lies in building complete solutions.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Talent and tooling demand in finance tilts toward technical, process-building skills.

insights.claim: Using the analogy of elevator operators (fully automated away because they only executed) versus airline pilots (more numerous after autopilot because they own the outcome), the guest argues workers who own outcomes gain from automation.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Framework for judging which job categories AI displaces versus augments.

insights.claim: The host observes mid-career professionals skilled with AI now do work themselves that they previously delegated to interns or junior analysts.
insights.speaker: Ash Bennington (host)
insights.so_what: Direct evidence of AI substituting for entry-level labor in finance.

insights.claim: The guest left his COO role at an a16z-backed startup (which raised over $30 million) because he felt his role was becoming less valuable as AI advanced, and says even software engineering demand is in decline.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Signals perceived erosion of value in traditional engineering and operating roles.

insights.claim: The guest's closing advice is to shorten the learn-to-apply feedback loop, claiming the most effective companies and people with AI are those that reduce the time from learning something to applying it.
insights.speaker: Austin Marchese (guest, ex-JP Morgan engineer, AI incubator founder)
insights.so_what: Speed of internal AI adoption may become a differentiator between companies.
